claims.text: The factors of production are the four types of resource a business combines in order to make goods or provide services: land, labour, capital and enterprise.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Land, as a factor of production, means the natural resources an operation draws on: the site it occupies, the water it uses, and the minerals, crops, timber or fish it takes from nature.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Labour, as a factor of production, means the physical and mental effort supplied by the people a business employs, and what that effort is worth to the operation depends on skill, training and motivation as much as on the number of people.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Capital, as a factor of production, means the man-made assets used to produce other goods and services - machinery, buildings, vehicles, tools and equipment - together with the money committed to acquiring them.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Enterprise, as a factor of production, means the act of bringing the other three factors together and bearing the risk that the venture loses money; it is supplied by the entrepreneur, or by managers acting for the owners.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The proportions in which a business combines the four factors are a management decision rather than a fixed recipe, so two businesses making a similar product may use very different mixes of land, labour, capital and enterprise.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Where one factor becomes scarcer or dearer, a business may substitute another factor for it - more machinery in place of costly labour, or more labour where equipment is expensive to buy and maintain - provided the technology of the process allows one to do the work of the other.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The transformational process is the sequence by which an operation converts inputs into outputs that are worth more to a customer than the same inputs were worth separately.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The process runs in three stages - inputs, transformation, outputs - and the inputs include the four factors of production together with bought-in materials and components, information, and in many services the customer.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Transformation may change the physical form of a material, move something to where it is wanted, hold it until it is wanted, or change its condition or its ownership; a service operation often transforms the customer, the customer's information or the customer's possessions rather than a material of its own.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The outputs of a transformational process include the goods or services the business sells and also by-products, scrap and waste, which carry disposal or reworking costs of their own.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The process is controlled by measuring the output against the standard set for it and feeding that result back, so that the inputs used or the steps of the transformation itself can be adjusted.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Added value is the difference between the price at which a product is sold and the cost of the bought-in materials and components used to make it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Added value per unit = selling price per unit - cost of bought-in materials and components per unit; total added value for a period = added value per unit x units sold in that period. The result is an amount of money, expressed in the currency of the business.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Operations raises added value from two directions at once: by making the output worth more to the buyer through design, quality, reliability, speed of delivery or service, and by lowering what is paid for bought-in inputs through better buying, less waste and less reworking.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Added value is not profit. It is the amount left to cover wages, power, rent, marketing, finance and every other cost the business carries, and only what remains after all of those have been met is profit.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The word contribution is used in this topic in its ordinary sense - the part operations plays in creating added value - and carries no formula. The costing sense of contribution, selling price minus variable cost per unit, belongs to the costs topic and is a different quantity.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Efficiency, effectiveness, productivity and sustainability are four separate tests of the same operation: how little resource it uses for the output it produces, whether it achieves the objectives set for it, how much output each unit of input yields, and whether it can be carried on into the long term.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The four measures can move in opposite directions, so an operation that improves on one may worsen on another - running a line faster raises output per employee while it may also raise the scrap rate - and a business that judges operations on a single measure can miss the cost appearing on the others.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Managers use the four measures together because each answers a question the others leave open, and the weight given to each depends on the objectives the business has set for the period.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Efficiency is the extent to which an operation produces its output with the minimum of resources, so that as little as possible is wasted.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Effectiveness is the extent to which an operation achieves the objectives that have been set for it, whatever quantity of resources it uses in doing so.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Efficiency asks about the ratio of output to the resources consumed; effectiveness asks whether the intended result was reached. Because they are different questions, an operation may be efficient without being effective, producing cheaply something that does not meet the objective, and effective without being efficient, meeting the objective at a cost the business need not have borne.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: One common measure of efficiency is average cost per unit = total cost of a period / output of that period, expressed in currency per unit. A fall in average cost, where quality and the mix of products are unchanged, indicates that the operation has become more efficient.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Productivity is output per unit of input over a stated period. It is a ratio, so it is reported as output per employee, per labour hour or per machine hour, and not as a total.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Production is the total quantity an operation produces; productivity is that quantity divided by the input used to produce it. Production can rise at the same time as productivity falls, if the extra output required a more than proportionate increase in the input.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A rise in productivity lowers the cost of that input per unit of output, provided the price paid for the input has not risen by as much or more; where a productivity rise is bought with a pay rise of the same proportion, cost per unit is unchanged.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Productivity can be raised by training, by better or better-maintained equipment, by improving the layout and sequence of the process so that less time is spent moving and waiting, and by changes to pay, job design and supervision that raise motivation.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Higher productivity turns into a lower total cost only where the extra output can be sold, or where the input can be reduced in step with it; otherwise the business holds unsold inventory or goes on paying for time it does not use.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Sustainability of operations means running the operation so that it can be carried on into the long term: using natural resources no faster than they are replaced, and keeping the environmental and social costs it imposes within limits it can go on meeting.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Sustainability of an operation is usually examined on three fronts: environmental - energy, water, materials, waste and emissions; social - safety, pay and conditions, and the effect on the communities around the site; and economic - whether the operation earns enough to keep itself going.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Common measures to improve the sustainability of operations include cutting energy and water used per unit, replacing non-renewable inputs with renewable ones, recycling and re-using materials, reducing scrap and reworking, designing products to last longer or to be repaired, and sourcing inputs closer to the point of use.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Some sustainability measures lower operating cost as well as environmental impact, because energy, water and materials that are not used are also not paid for; the size of that saving depends on how much of the input the measure actually removes.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Where a sustainability measure requires capital spending, its financial case rests on the payback period - the outlay divided by the annual saving - and on whether that saving continues, so a measure with a short payback is easier to justify than one whose saving is small relative to what it costs to install.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Labour productivity = total output in a period / number of employees in that period. It is measured in units of output per employee per period, and the period must be stated for the figure to mean anything.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Where employees work unequal hours, labour productivity is better measured as total output / total labour hours worked, which gives output per labour hour and is not distorted by part-time or overtime working.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Labour cost per unit = total labour cost of the period / output of that period, expressed in currency per unit. It falls as labour productivity rises, so long as the wage bill does not rise in the same proportion.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A labour productivity figure means little on its own. It is read against the same operation's earlier figures, against the target set for it, or against another business producing comparable output by comparable methods.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Labour productivity counts quantity and not quality, so units later reworked, scrapped or returned are still counted in the output; the figure is also raised by better machinery rather than by harder work, and a headcount that treats part-time and seasonal staff as whole employees understates the labour actually used.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The two commonest errors in measuring labour productivity are inverting the formula, dividing employees by output instead of output by employees, and reporting total output and calling it productivity.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Measures that cut the energy, water and materials an operation uses, or the waste it produces, lower its operating costs once they are working, and that saving continues for as long as the measure stays in use.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Improved sustainability may widen the market a business can sell into, because some retail chains, exporters and public bodies set environmental conditions on the suppliers they buy from, and it may help recruitment and retention where employees place a value on it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Most sustainability measures require capital spending, retraining and a period of disruption before any saving appears, so cash flow and profit are likely to worsen before they improve.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Certified, recycled or locally sourced inputs sometimes cost more per unit than the inputs they replace, so a sustainability measure can raise the cost of every unit the business makes rather than lower it.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Whether a measure to improve sustainability is worth making turns on the size and durability of the saving set against the outlay, on whether the business can finance that outlay without straining its cash, and on whether its own customers and regulators place a value on the change.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A capital intensive operation is one in which machinery and equipment do most of the work, so that capital costs form the larger share of total cost and relatively few employees are needed for the output produced.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Machinery repeats the same action to the same tolerance for as long as it is maintained, so a capital intensive operation tends to produce more uniform output, with fewer defects and less reworking, than one that depends on people repeating the same action by hand.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Where volume is high and steady, a capital intensive operation tends to have the lower cost per unit, because the heavy fixed cost of the equipment is spread over a large number of units and little labour time is used on each one; at low volumes that same fixed cost raises average cost sharply.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Equipment can be run for long or continuous hours and its output can be raised quickly once it is installed, which suits demand that is large and predictable; it also reduces the disruption an operation suffers from absence or industrial action.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The outlay on a capital intensive operation is large and is committed before any of the output is sold, and it then becomes a cost that must be covered whatever the level of output achieved.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A capital intensive operation is harder to change: altering the specification usually means re-tooling or reprogramming, a breakdown stops a whole line rather than one worker's station, and the equipment loses value both through wear and through newer models coming onto the market.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A labour intensive operation is one in which people do most of the work, so that labour costs form the larger share of total cost and relatively little capital equipment is used for the output produced.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The initial outlay on a labour intensive operation is smaller, so it can be started with less finance, and its scale can be raised or lowered without committing or stranding large sums of capital.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: People can be moved between tasks and re-instructed within a day, so a labour intensive operation handles varied, customised or irregular work more readily than equipment that has been set up for one specification.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Where the value of a product rests on craft, judgement or personal contact with the customer, labour is the factor that creates that value, and equipment substitutes for it only in part.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Labour cost per unit in a labour intensive operation tends to be higher at large volumes, and it rises directly whenever wage rates rise, while output varies with absence, turnover, fatigue and individual skill, so uniform quality is harder to hold.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The choice between capital intensive and labour intensive operation is a matter of degree rather than of kind: most operations mix the two, and the sensible mix depends on the volume and variety of the output, the relative cost of labour and equipment where the business operates, and the finance it can raise.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Job production is making one item, or one complete order, at a time to a customer's own requirements, and finishing it before the next is begun.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Batch production is making identical items in groups, with the whole group completing one stage of the process before it moves to the next, and the equipment reset between one group and the next.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Flow production is the continuous movement of identical items through a fixed sequence of stages, each stage adding something to every item, with output coming off the end for as long as the line runs.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Mass customisation is the use of flow methods to produce items that differ from one another in specified ways, achieved by assembling standard modules in different combinations or by leaving the varying work to a late stage of the line.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The production methods are compared along the same dimensions: the volume of output, the variety of specification allowed, the cost per unit, the skill and flexibility asked of the workforce, the capital equipment required, and how quickly the operation can be switched to something different.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Job production allows any specification the customer asks for and can command a higher price for that, and it uses skilled, motivated workers on a whole task; its cost per unit is high, because skilled time and equipment are devoted to a single item, and total output is low.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Batch production spreads each set-up over a whole group, so its cost per unit is lower than job production while some variety is kept; the price is the time lost setting up at every change of group, and the part-finished stock that waits between stages, tying up money and space.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Flow production gives the lowest cost per unit at high volume and a very uniform product, and it can be largely automated; it requires a large capital outlay, allows little variety once installed, and a stoppage at any one point halts the whole line.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Mass customisation offers buyers a choice of specification without the unit cost of job production, but it requires the product to be designed as modules, and a system able to track which variant belongs to which order; the number of variants that can be offered is limited by what that system can handle.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Moving from one production method to another usually requires new equipment and a new layout, so the business commits capital, and often borrows to do so, before the new method has produced anything to sell.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Output usually falls while the change is made, because the old arrangement is taken out while the new one is installed and tested, so the business has to build up finished stock beforehand or accept that some orders are late or lost.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The skills the operation needs change with the method, so staff have to be retrained; a move towards flow methods narrows many jobs to one repeated task, which some employees experience as a loss of skill and interest, and that may raise labour turnover and weaken motivation.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A change of method usually changes the number of people required, so the business may face redundancy payments, statutory consultation with employees or their representatives, and a spell of poor industrial relations while the change is negotiated.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Output per employee on a new method usually starts below the level it will eventually reach, because operators and supervisors are still learning the process, so unit costs are higher and defects more frequent in the first months of running.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A move towards flow production raises the share of total cost that is fixed, so the business becomes more exposed if the forecast volume does not appear: the same capital has to be covered from fewer units.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Changing method can change what the business is able to sell, because a move from job or batch towards flow narrows the range of specifications it can offer, and customers who bought it for that flexibility may go elsewhere.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The problems of changing method are reduced where the change is phased - one line converted and proved first, employees consulted early, and the existing method kept running until the new one reaches its planned output - although phasing itself costs money and delays the saving.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 9609 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
